questions.prompt: Explain eShopOnWeb's request pipeline as the framework guide models it: how a request travels through middleware and who decides the order, where authentication and authorization must sit relative to routing and why, what each middleware can do around next, and which middleware could stop a GET / before the page handler runs.

keyPoints.text: A request flows through an ordered chain of middleware, each wrapping next, until an endpoint handles it.
keyPoints.quote: each wrapping `next`, until an endpoint handles it.

keyPoints.text: The order is code you control.
keyPoints.quote: The order is code you control

keyPoints.text: Authentication runs before authorization, and both after routing so endpoint metadata exists.
keyPoints.quote: authentication must run *before* authorization, both *after* routing (so endpoint metadata exists)

keyPoints.text: In Web/Program.cs, UseRouting comes before UseAuthentication and UseAuthorization.
Each middleware can act before calling next, act after it returns, or short-circuit (a 401 skips the rest).
keyPoints.quote: Each can act before calling `next`, act after it returns, or short-circuit

keyPoints.text: Static-file or auth middleware can short-circuit before the page handler runs.
keyPoints.quote: static-file or auth middleware can short-circuit before the page handler runs.

questions.prompt: How does eShopOnWeb build its object graph and read configuration? Explain what you register and how the container constructs objects, give the repo's example of each of the three lifetimes, and describe the options pattern versus the configuration pitfall the guide lists.

keyPoints.text: You register interface-to-implementation mappings once and the container builds everything by constructor injection.
keyPoints.quote: the container constructs everything via constructor injection.

keyPoints.text: Singleton: one instance for the app, used for the stateless UriComposer.
keyPoints.quote: one instance for the app. Used for stateless `UriComposer`

keyPoints.text: Scoped: one per request, as for the repositories and the basket and order services.
Transient: a new instance each time, as for EmailSender.
Configuration binds to typed objects with Configure<T>(section), then code injects IOptions<T>.
The pitfall is reading config with stringly-typed configuration["key"] instead of options.
keyPoints.quote: Reading config with stringly-typed `configuration["key"]` instead of options

questions.prompt: What is the EF Core mental model in this repo? Explain what a DbContext is and what SaveChanges does, when LINQ against a DbSet actually runs, which part of the catalog page query runs in SQL versus in memory, what Include buys, and what you risk by trusting the in-memory provider.

keyPoints.text: A DbContext is a unit of work: load, mutate, and SaveChanges computes and commits the diff in one transaction.
keyPoints.quote: You load entities, mutate them, and `SaveChanges` computes and commits the diff in one transaction.

keyPoints.text: LINQ against a DbSet builds an expression tree that EF translates to SQL and runs when materialized.
keyPoints.quote: LINQ against a `DbSet` builds an expression tree that EF translates to SQL and runs when materialized.

keyPoints.text: A spec's Where/Skip/Take run in SQL; the later Select into a view model runs in memory.
keyPoints.quote: a spec's `Where/Skip/Take` run in SQL; a later `.Select` into a view model runs in memory

keyPoints.text: Include/ThenInclude fetch related data in the same query, the antidote to N+1.
keyPoints.quote: fetch related data in the same query

keyPoints.text: The in-memory provider does not enforce real constraints, so it hides some bugs.
keyPoints.quote: the in-memory provider doesn't enforce real constraints, so it hides some bugs.
